item.title: Energy Brief: China Rare Earth Suppliers Halt Some US Shipments Ahead of Xi Visit; Hormuz Lull Ends as Brent Nears $95
item.description:
Chinese rare earth exporters are refusing some US shipments weeks before Xi Jinping visits Washington, while the Strait of Hormuz returns to active hostilities and a refining crunch pushes Brent toward $95. The Russia-China pipeline file also moved as Novak revived the Power of Baikal talks.
► China Rare Earth Suppliers Freeze Some US Shipments Ahead of Xi Visit Some Chinese rare earth suppliers are declining to ship to the US for fear of repercussions from Beijing, three sources told Reuters, keeping access to critical materials a live problem weeks before President Xi Jinping is due in Washington on Septem Why it matters: This is a quiet form of leverage Beijing can calibrate precisely — refusing specific shipments without an embargo — timed ahead of the September 24 summit. It keeps rare earth supply risk live for US automakers and defense firms even as US officials want a smooth visit.
► Hormuz Returns to Active Hostilities as Transit Slumps The month-long lull in US-Iran fighting ended this week, with the US resuming attacks on Iranian targets along the Strait of Hormuz and tensions over the waterway rising again, according to USNI News. Why it matters: The return to strikes confirms neither side has an off-ramp that sticks; Vance's condition effectively rules out talks while shipping remains a target. The persistence of dark-fleet traffic shows sanctions and blockade are being eroded by evasion, not stopped.
► Record Diesel Prices Push Brent Toward $95 Refined products, not crude, are driving this oil rally. US retail diesel hit a record $5. 848 per gallon on a full-day national average (Reuters, Sept 3), while regular gasoline sits at about $4. 07, according to GasBuddy. OilPrice. Why it matters: The gap between record diesel and softer gasoline shows the war is hitting supply chains directly — diesel funds freight, agriculture and construction — so the economic bite of this conflict arrives at the consumer register rather than only at the pump.

Why it matters: OPEC+ holding quotas while prices climb means the group is choosing restraint over capturing war-driven upside — a posture that keeps spare capacity in reserve and quietly signals it cannot flood a market whose flows are physically disrupted.

But with output already slipping and refinery losses from drone strikes, Russia is negotiating from a weakened supply position.

item.title: Energy Brief: Global Refining Crunch to Keep Fuel Prices High Into 2027 as China's Oil Demand Falls 9%
item.description:
Damaged Middle East and Russian refineries cannot be offset by spare capacity elsewhere, analysts warn, even as China's oil consumption posts its sharpest quarterly decline in years. The Iran war is tightening the product market even while headline crude stays high, and Baghdad quietly doubles Hormuz exports at steep discounts.
► Refining Crunch Is the Real Story Behind High Fuel Prices The war's biggest market effect is no longer just crude supply — it is the loss of refining capacity. Why it matters: Crude may be in surplus, but the diesel and gasoline the world actually consumes are short. This reframes the war's cost: even a de-escalation in the Gulf would not quickly restore fuel supply, because refining assets take years to rebuild.
► China's Oil Consumption Falls 9% as EVs and Electrified Trucking Bite China's oil consumption fell 9% year over year in the second quarter, according to an analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) cited by OilPrice. com. Why it matters: China, the world's largest crude importer, is structurally reducing its oil appetite just as the Gulf war spikes prices. For producers, this 9% demand decline, not the war headlines, is the number that shapes the medium-term balance.
► Russia's Oil Revenue Sinks as Urals Falls Back to $59 Russia collected 326. 2 billion rubles (about $3. 76 billion) in net oil revenue in August, down 22% year over year and the lowest monthly total since February, OilPrice. com reported, citing Russian tax data. Why it matters: The Iran war's price rally briefly masked the strain on Russia's budget, but Ukrainian strikes on refineries and export terminals are now grinding down both output and revenue. Moscow's war-chest cushion is thinning at a time of heavy spending.
► Iraq Quietly Doubles Hormuz Exports at Steep Discounts OPEC's second-largest producer more than doubled crude exports via the Strait of Hormuz in August to about 2. 34 million bpd from 1. Why it matters: Iraqi crude is re-entering the market at discounts that suit India and China's heavy-crude refiners, a partial, Iran-permitted normalization of Gulf flows. It shows trade rerouting around Iran's de facto chokepoint control is happening cargo by cargo, not all at once.
► Japan's Biggest Tanker Operator Sees Hormuz Disruptions Dragging Into Next Year Mitsui OSK Lines, the world's largest tanker operator, now expects Hormuz shipping disruptions to continue well past the end of the year, its CEO Jotaro Tamura told Bloomberg. Why it matters: The shipping industry's own risk assessment is the most concrete signal that a return to normal Gulf logistics is months away. This hardens the market view that tightness — and the refining crunch — are not short-term.
► Shell Closes $16.5B ARC Resources Deal, Deepening Western Exposure to Montney Shell completed its $16. 5 billion acquisition of Canada's ARC Resources, the company announced Wednesday. Why it matters: With Gulf and Russian barrels disrupted and refining tight, Western majors are consolidating secure North American supply. M&A is the quiet counterpart to the war-driven scramble — buying low-cost, geopolitically safe barrels rather than relying on chokepoint logistics.
► Venezuela Deal Runs Into Creditor and Legitimacy Questions; US Uranium Output Triples but Imports Still Dominate Two transition-adjacent stories. Why it matters: Washington's Venezuela overture to add Western-controlled barrels faces the same legal and political fog that has blocked foreign capital for two decades. And on nuclear fuel, tripling a tiny base leaves the US dependent on imports — a supply-chain exposure the transition debate keeps circling back to.

item.title: Energy Brief: OPEC+ Set to Hold Output Steady as War Erodes Its Market Power; India Steps Up Russian ESPO Imports
item.description:
Seven core OPEC+ members meet Sunday expected to keep October quotas unchanged, even as the Iran war undercuts the group's ability to move prices. Meanwhile India is quietly absorbing more Russian Far East crude as China pulls back and Hormuz stays choked.
► OPEC+ Holds Steady as the War Erodes Its Leverage OPEC+ is expected to leave its oil production policy unchanged for October when seven core members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — meet online Sunday, Reuters reported Wednesday, citing three sources. Why it matters: The war has quietly hollowed out OPEC+'s central function — managing the market. With Gulf barrels trapped behind Hormuz, the group's quota decisions are becoming secondary to physical supply disruptions, and the 2027 baseline fight is exposing internal fractures (UAE exit, Venezuela doubts, Iraq demands).
► Hormuz: Two Filipino Sailors Killed, Saudi Formally Accuses Iran Two Filipino crew members died from Monday's attack on the Saudi oil tanker Sidr, operated by state shipping firm Bahri, Bahri confirmed Wednesday. Why it matters: The first confirmed deaths of tanker crew in this phase of the war sharply raise the stakes for Riyadh, which has so far avoided direct military retaliation. With transit down to four ships a day, the physical supply picture — not OPEC+ targets — is what is setting prices.
► India Steps Up Russian ESPO Imports as China Pulls Back India raised its purchases of Russia's Far East ESPO blend in the first seven months of 2026 as China backed out of the spot market early in the Iran war and Middle East deliveries slumped with the Hormuz closure, OilPrice. Why it matters: The ESPO shift shows how the war is re-sorting Asian crude flows: China retreats from spot purchases, India backfills, and Russia's Pacific export route becomes a more important outlet as its western and Gulf-facing logistics are disrupted. It is a logistics-driven reshuffle, not a strategic realignment.
► Qatar and UAE Turn to Rare LNG Ship-to-Ship Transfers Three LNG carriers loaded from Qatar and the UAE transferred their cargoes onto other vessels outside the Strait of Hormuz in the past month — a highly unusual move for LNG, Reuters reported Wednesday, citing Vortexa and Kpler vessel-tracking data. Why it matters: Ship-to-ship transfers are a workaround, not a fix — they keep a trickle of Qatari and Emirati LNG moving but cannot restore normal volumes. The LNG market is absorbing the Hormuz blockage far worse than crude, and the price signal is now showing up in both Asia and Europe.
► Chevron Puts a Number on Venezuela: $7 Billion, 600,000 bpd Chevron will invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela over the next five years and more than double its production there to about 600,000 bpd, Reuters reported Wednesday. Why it matters: This converts the earlier 'significant size' Venezuela agreements into a concrete commercial commitment. Chevron is moving first and fast to lock in Orinoco acreage and terms before rivals return, positioning itself as the anchor of a U. S. -directed Venezuelan rebuild.
► Saudi Arabia Aims to Free 1 Million bpd of Domestic Oil Burn Saudi Arabia wants to displace more than 1 million bpd of domestic liquid-fuel consumption by 2030, primarily through natural gas and renewables, with nuclear playing a larger role after 2030, OilPrice. com reported, citing Arab News and IEA data. Why it matters: Every barrel Saudi Arabia stops burning domestically is a barrel available for export — a quiet way to add supply without raising quotas. The U. S. -Saudi nuclear deal ties Riyadh's post-2030 power strategy to American suppliers, a strategic foothold that also frees more Saudi crude for the export market.

item.title: Energy Brief: US Takes 35% Stake in Venezuela's 65-Billion-Barrel Oil Deal via Pentagon Office; Hormuz Hostilities Resume as Two Saudi Tankers Struck
item.description:
Washington formalized a sweeping Venezuela oil arrangement — 17 fields, 100-year concessions, a Pentagon equity stake — while renewed US-Iran strikes and tanker attacks near Hormuz pushed Brent above $92 and European gas to six-month highs.
► The Venezuela Deal: Pentagon Equity, 100-Year Concessions, 65 Billion Barrels The White House released a fact sheet on Aug. 31 detailing the US-Venezuela oil agreement President Trump first announced on Aug. 28. Why it matters: This is a new model of US energy statecraft: a defense-investment office taking equity in a foreign oil venture to secure offtake, rather than sanctions or traditional diplomacy.
► Hormuz Hostilities Resume: Two Saudi Tankers Struck, US Hits IRGC Targets The month-long lull in the US-Iran war broke Monday. Why it matters: The recovery in Hormuz flows — the key reason oil had eased — is now at risk of reversing. The new tanker-for-tanker policy directly targets Iran's oil export revenue, escalating the economic dimension of the conflict even as the military exchanges resume.
► QatarEnergy Extends LNG Force Majeure; European Gas Hits Six-Month High QatarEnergy has again extended force majeure on LNG deliveries to Europe and Asia as regular shipping through Hormuz remains largely halted, Euronews reports. Why it matters: Qatar's prolonged absence from the LNG market is the quiet structural driver of high gas prices on both sides of the world. With Hormuz flows again under threat, buyers face a winter where the single largest LNG supplier remains effectively offline.
► Russia Doubles Its LNG Dark Fleet as Arctic LNG 2 Ramps for China Russia has nearly doubled the fleet of tankers serving its US-sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project in under a year, from 11 ships at the end of December to at least 20, according to a Bloomberg analysis of ship-tracking data. Why it matters: Russia is quietly rebuilding its gas export machine around a single sanctioned project and a single buyer, with Washington declining to enforce the previous administration's restrictions. The dark-fleet build-out is a direct test of whether US sanctions on Russian energy still bite.
► SCO Summit: Xi-Putin Gas Talks and a Multipolar Energy Bloc At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met Monday to discuss bilateral relations including, per the Russian side, gas — keeping the long-stalled Power of Siberia 2 pipeline on the agenda, Bloomberg a Why it matters: The SCO is consolidating as an energy-aligned bloc of sanctioned and non-Western producers. Power of Siberia 2 remains stalled on price, but the political scaffolding around a Russia-China-Iran energy axis is being reinforced at a moment when Hormuz disruption raises the value of overland alternatives.
■ The Bottom Line Two forces moved energy markets today. Washington formalized an unprecedented Venezuela arrangement — a Pentagon investment office taking a 35% equity stake in a 65-billion-barrel venture with 100-year concessions — signaling the US is building a non-Hormuz supply hedge through direct state equity rather than sanctions. Simultaneously, the US-Iran war resumed in earnest: two Saudi tankers were struck near Hormuz, CENTCOM confirmed strikes on IRGC targets, and a new tanker-for-tanker policy targets Iran's oil revenue. Brent pushed above $92, European gas hit six-month highs, and QatarEnergy's LNG force majeure — now in its sixth month — keeps the world's largest LNG supplier offline. The Venezuela deal is a long-term hedge; the Hormuz escalation is the immediate risk.

item.title: Energy Brief: Asian Refiners Turn to Argentina as War Reroutes Global Oil Flows; China LNG Imports Set to Drop 18% on Record Prices
item.description:
The Iran war's supply shock is now reshaping trade routes far beyond Hormuz: Asian buyers are sourcing chokepoint-free crude from Argentina, Asia is filling Africa's diesel gap, and record LNG prices are starting to destroy Chinese demand. Europe gas hit its highest level since 2023 as US-Iran strikes resumed.
► The War's Supply Shock Reroutes Global Trade Flows Asian crude importers including China, Japan and South Korea have turned to buying oil from as far as Argentina to offset Middle East supply losses, anonymous traders told Bloomberg on Monday. Why it matters: The war is no longer just a chokepoint story — it is forcing a permanent-looking reconfiguration of global crude and fuel trade, with Argentina and Asia emerging as new suppliers of last resort.
► Aramco Keeps Saudi Crude Flowing to China via Ship-to-Ship Handoffs Saudi Aramco is offering more September crude to Asian buyers through ship-to-ship transfers outside Hormuz, according to Reuters, after shipping data showed Saudi barrels moving through the strait with tracking systems switched off. Why it matters: Saudi Arabia is absorbing the Hormuz risk itself to keep its largest customer supplied, a workaround that keeps barrels moving but signals the strait remains far from normal.
► Europe Gas Hits Highest Level Since 2023 as US-Iran Strikes Resume European benchmark natural gas prices jumped 5% in early Monday trade, with the Dutch TTF topping 70 euros ($81. 20) per MWh — the highest front-month level in more than three and a half years, since January 2023, Oilprice. com reported. Why it matters: With storage at a two-decade low and Qatari term deliveries absent, Europe enters winter structurally exposed to any further supply shock — and gas prices are already pricing that risk in.
► Record LNG Prices Start Destroying Chinese Demand China's LNG imports are on track to slump 18% in August from a year earlier, to about 5. 2 million tons, bucking a three-month trend of growing purchases, per Kpler estimates cited by Bloomberg. Why it matters: The first clear sign of demand destruction in the world's largest LNG buyer — a signal that sustained high prices are now curbing consumption, not just reallocating it.
► Chevron, ONGC and GE Vernova Near Final Venezuela Energy Deals Chevron, India's ONGC, GE Vernova, Eni and GeoPark are preparing to sign final energy agreements in Venezuela, Reuters reported Monday, citing five sources. Why it matters: Venezuela is moving from state control to a contract model that lets foreign firms capture export revenue directly — a structural shift that could meaningfully add non-Hormuz supply to a tight global market.
► Critical Minerals and Nuclear Fuel Tighten: Lithium Profits, Uranium Surge Lithium miners are reporting strong first-half profits on surging battery storage demand, Bloomberg reported. Why it matters: The energy-security scramble is feeding directly into transition and nuclear supply chains — lithium and uranium are both tightening as importers hedge against fossil-fuel chokepoint risk.
► Iran-Hormuz Update: Strikes Resume After Month-Long Lull US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island inside the Strait of Hormuz after the IRGC were observed 'preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait,' per a US Central Command spokesperson, Oilprice. com reported. Why it matters: The month-long lull is over, but the market's muted reaction — oil up only ~3. 6% — suggests traders have largely priced in a conflict that keeps disrupting supply without fully closing the strait.
■ The Bottom Line The Iran war's supply shock is now visibly reshaping global energy trade beyond the chokepoint itself: Asian refiners are sourcing chokepoint-free crude from Argentina, Asia is filling Africa's diesel gap, Saudi Arabia is absorbing Hormuz risk via ship-to-ship handoffs to keep China supplied, and rec...

item.title: Energy Brief: US Strikes Iranian Rocket Launchers at Larak Island, Ending Month-Long Hormuz Lull as Tanker Hit Near Khasab; Europe's Gas Storage Hits 13-Year Low
item.description:
The US military struck Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday — the first direct US attack on Iranian positions in over a month — after Tehran prepared to lay sea mines, and Iran retaliated with missile fire at US bases in Jordan. Brent crude climbed toward $90 as Europe's gas reserves fell to their lowest level since 2013.
► Hormuz: US Ends Month-Long Lull With Strike on Larak Island The US military struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, August 30, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) was observed preparing to launch rockets carrying sea mines into the waterway, a US Why it matters: The strike signals Washington will use force to prevent Iran from re-establishing its ability to threaten Hormuz shipping, but analysts note the strait is physically open — reduced traffic is driven by the risk of attack, which mine-clearing alone cannot eliminate.
► Oil: Brent Climbs Toward $90 as Gulf Attacks Resume Oil prices rose on Monday, August 31, after fresh fighting erupted in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude gained 1. 6% to $89. 50 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate rose 1. 5% to $84. 63, according to CNBC-TV18. Why it matters: The renewed tit-for-tat shows the market's 'war premium' is not fading — it is re-pricing on each escalation. With the US-Iran conflict showing no off-ramp, oil remains structurally exposed to Hormuz risk, and the Venezuela deal's promise of lower prices has so far been outweighed by Middle East risk.
► Europe: Gas Storage at Lowest Since 2013 as 'Winter Panic' Builds EU gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level since 2013, feeding a 'winter panic' among traders, The Guardian reported, as cited by Press TV. Why it matters: The shortfall stems from weak commercial incentives to inject gas now for winter resale, compounded by Hormuz disruption to Qatari LNG and EU sanctions on Russian supply. Low storage raises the risk of sharp winter price volatility, and Germany's shortfall has knock-on effects across Europe because it holds the largest storage system.
► Venezuela: US Moves to Control 65 Billion Barrels, Refill SPR Washington is moving to take direct control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves through a proposed 100-year concession spanning 17 fields, per a Bloomberg report cited by CNBC-TV18. Why it matters: The deal would make the new US-controlled entity the second-largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, and more than double US oil reserves.
► SCO Summit in Bishkek: Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian Meet as Russia Looks East Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian convened in Bishkek on August 31 for the two-day Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit marking its 25th anniversary, RFE/RL reported. Why it matters: The summit is a venue for Russia, China and Iran to coordinate on energy and sanctions circumvention, but its practical limits are clear: it cannot protect members from secondary sanctions. The Rosatom nuclear deal with Iran is a strategic signal of deepening Russia-Iran energy cooperation even as both face Western pressure.
► Global South: Bangladesh's Energy Import Bill Doubles as LNG Crunch Bites Bangladesh's energy import bill reached $10. Why it matters: Bangladesh illustrates how the global energy shock is hitting the Global South hardest — a doubling import bill, chronic load-shedding and stalled investment. The LNG supply crunch, worsened by Hormuz disruption and rising prices, is forcing a poor importer to ration gas between power, fertilizer and industry.

item.title: Energy Brief: Power of Siberia 2 Back on Putin-Xi Agenda at Bishkek SCO Summit as Modi Courts Central Asia; Iran War Adds $330B to Global Energy Bills
item.description:
The SCO's 25th-anniversary summit in Kyrgyzstan brings Russia, China, India and Iran together with the stalled Power of Siberia 2 pipeline on the Putin-Xi bilateral agenda, while new CREA data quantifies the Iran war's $330 billion toll on global energy importers.
► Bishkek SCO Summit Puts Power of Siberia 2 Back on the Table The Kremlin confirmed on Friday that Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold bilateral talks on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, with the long-stalled Power of Siberia 2 gas pipeline among the items on the agenda, according to Why it matters: A Power of Siberia 2 breakthrough would lock Russia's energy future to China for decades and reshape Eurasian gas flows, while the SCO's collective posture on Iran signals a coordinated non-Western bloc position on the Gulf crisis.
► Modi's Central Asia Tour: Uranium, Rare Earths and Chabahar Integration PM Modi's four-day Central Asia visit, which began Saturday, pairs a state visit to Uzbekistan with the Bishkek SCO summit, with energy security and critical minerals at the core of the agenda, per Firstpost. Why it matters: India is using the SCO platform to build an alternative energy and minerals supply chain through Central Asia, reducing dependence on Hormuz-linked routes and Chinese-dominated processing, while positioning itself as a Eurasian power broker ahead of the BRICS summit.
► Iran War Added $330 Billion to Global Energy Import Bills New data from the Finland-based think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates the Iran war added $330 billion to global oil, fuel and LNG import bills between March and August, with crude accounting for $164. Why it matters: The CREA figures put a hard number on the war's economic cost and show the burden is falling hardest on import-dependent economies, not the belligerents — a dynamic that will shape winter politics in Europe and Asia.
► Venezuela Deal Details Emerge: 25-Year Term, 1.5M bpd Target, OPEC Exit Weighed Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez said the US energy agreement will run 25 years and target crude output of more than 1. 5 million barrels per day across 17 strategic oilfields, per Reuters. Why it matters: The deal's concrete terms — 25 years, 1. 5M bpd, a 55% US output share — and the OPEC exit question would, if realized, fundamentally reorder the Western Hemisphere oil map and further erode OPEC's cohesion at a moment of Gulf disruption.
► UK Takes Rights to Half of Devon Tungsten Output in £71M State Bet The UK's National Wealth Fund is investing up to £71 million in Tungsten West to restart the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon, Europe's largest tungsten deposit, according to the Financial Times and The Times via Finanznachrichten. Why it matters: Governments are moving from subsidy programs to directly securing future output of critical minerals — a state-capitalist turn in Western supply security that signals tungsten, like rare earths, is becoming a strategic commodity rather than a market one.
► India's Argentina Minerals Push Goes Beyond Lithium India's state-owned Khanij Bidesh India Limited (KABIL) is deepening its Argentine footprint, with the fourth India-Argentina Joint Trade Committee meeting in Buenos Aires on August 24 reviewing progress on lithium blocks in Catamarca and exploring e Why it matters: India is trying to build a vertically integrated lithium-to-battery supply chain outside Chinese control, but execution delays show how hard it is to convert overseas mineral rights into actual production — a cautionary counterpoint to the US and UK state-backed pushes.

item.description:
Ship-tracking data shows Gulf oil flows recovering to roughly two-thirds of prewar levels via tanker shuttling and sales outside the strait, even as LNG traffic remains at a standstill and Qatar extends force majeure into November. President Trump formally announced an agreement giving US companies majority control of 65+ billion barrels of Venezuela's proven reserves.
► Hormuz Oil Flows Rebound Even as Tanker Traffic Stays Subdued The Iran war is entering its seventh month with a striking divergence at the Strait of Hormuz: oil volumes are flowing again, but actual vessel traffic is not. Why it matters: This is the first sustained evidence that oil markets can partially reroute around the chokepoint — explaining why Brent has slid rather than spiked. But the recovery depends on costly shuttling and stealth, not a normal reopening, so the constraint on Gulf exports is easing slowly, not ending.
► LNG Stays Fully Blocked as Qatar Extends Force Majeure Through November Unlike crude, liquefied natural gas cannot be shuttle-shipped through Hormuz and reloaded, and Friday brought confirmation the impasse will persist: reports cited by Oilprice. Why it matters: The oil-gas split is the real story of the war's seventh month: the market can improvise around Hormuz for oil, but the gas trade has no such workaround. That leaves Europe and Asia competing for scarce LNG just as winter approaches, with Qatar's cargoes trapped behind the strait.
► Trump Formally Announced Venezuela Deal for Control of 65 Billion Barrels President Donald Trump on Friday announced an unprecedented agreement granting US companies majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves — about a fifth of the country's total — through a partnership with privat Why it matters: The deal converts an intervention into a permanent supply fixture for US refineries at a moment the strategic reserve is at a 40-year low. But the missing legal framework, the state-control question and the taxpayer cost Trump denies are all unresolved, meaning the headline number is bigger than the reality so far.

Why it matters: The debate over whether pipelines can replace Hormuz is central to how markets price the war's duration. Bessent's timeline assumes infrastructure that doesn't exist yet; the IEA and company plans suggest a partial, multi-year shift at best — leaving a persistent premium on Gulf crude.

item.title: Energy Brief: US Nears Deal for Stake in Venezuelan Oil Fields as OPEC+ Loses Market Sway to China
item.description:
Washington is closing in on a deal to lock in long-term access to Venezuelan crude — a move that could reshape the Western Hemisphere's oil map — while a Reuters analysis shows OPEC+ has lost its grip on prices six months into the Iran war, with China filling the vacuum.
► US Moves to Lock In Venezuelan Oil as Strategic Reserves Sit at 40-Year Low The Trump administration is working on a deal to secure long-term US access to a group of Venezuelan oilfields, Reuters reports, citing insiders who say an agreement could be signed and made public soon. Why it matters: This is Washington converting a military intervention into a permanent supply arrangement — effectively annexing the world's largest proven crude reserves into the US energy base. It also signals a shift in how the US thinks about energy security: not just sanctions and reserves, but direct ownership of foreign production.
► OPEC+ Loses Its Grip on Prices as China Fills the Power Vacuum Six months into the Iran war, OPEC+ is confronting a structural loss of influence, according to a Reuters analysis published Thursday. Why it matters: The cartel that spent decades setting the price of oil is now a paper tiger on supply. With the UAE gone and Gulf exporters physically constrained, the marginal price-setter is increasingly China's demand — a quiet but profound transfer of market power away from the producers' alliance.
► Hormuz Diplomacy Stalls as Trump Rejects June Ceasefire Terms Oil prices firmed Thursday after the Wall Street Journal reported that President Trump told mediators he was not interested in returning to the terms of a June ceasefire deal with Iran, dampening hopes that an Iran-Oman revenue-sharing arrangement ov Why it matters: The diplomatic window that briefly opened in June has closed. Washington is betting on sanctions and blockade pressure rather than a negotiated reopening of Hormuz, which means the physical constraint on Gulf exports — and the price premium it carries — is likely to persist into the autumn.
► Asia's Soft Imports Challenge US Claims of a Hormuz Rebound Asia, the biggest market for Gulf crude, is set to import 23. 12 million barrels per day in August, slightly down from 23. 36 million bpd in July, per Kpler data cited by Reuters columnist Clyde Russell. Imports from the Middle East inched up to 11. Why it matters: The gap between official US claims of a rebound and the actual shipping data matters because it shapes market expectations. If the rebound is overstated, the market is underpricing the persistence of the Hormuz constraint — and the risk of a sharper price move when reality catches up.

item.title: Energy Brief: Ukraine's Drone War Cuts Deep Into Russian Refining: Ust-Luga Terminal Hit, Moscow Now Imports Indian Gasoline

item.description:
A new Sunni defence pact reshapes Gulf security calculations just as Iran and Oman confirm a Hormuz framework deal that Tehran says won't fully reopen the strait. Ukraine drones hit two Russian refineries and shadow fleet vessels, while European gas storage sits at its lowest since 2011.
► Makkah Joint Defence Agreement: A New Sunni Security Architecture Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on Friday, August 7, stipulating that an armed attack on any of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against all. Why it matters: This is the first formal three-way defence pact among major Sunni powers that explicitly links an attack on one to a response by all — a qualitative shift from bilateral security understandings. It creates a new security bloc alongside (and potentially in tension with) the US security umbrella in the Gulf.
► Iran Confirms Hormuz Framework Deal; Seeks to Bar US and Israeli Vessels Iran confirmed on August 8 that a framework agreement with Oman on managing Strait of Hormuz transit has been reached, with final details to be announced soon, according to Iran's foreign ministry and Moneycontrol. Why it matters: A Hormuz framework exists on paper but the gap between what Iran calls a deal and what the US would accept remains vast — Iran wants to exclude US/Israeli shipping and retain transit controls, while Washington demands unconditional reopening.
► Ukraine Drones Hit Two Russian Refineries and Shadow Fleet Vessels Ukraine struck two Russian oil refineries in a coordinated long-range drone attack on August 6-7, according to the Kyiv Independent and United24 Media. Why it matters: Ukraine is now systematically targeting both the production side (refineries) and the export side (shadow fleet vessels) of Russia's oil revenue machine. The shadow fleet strikes, if sustained, could be more consequential than refinery hits — they threaten the sanctions-evasion infrastructure that keeps Russian oil flowing to global markets.
► European Gas Storage at Lowest Since 2011 as Winter Approaches European gas storage has fallen to 57% capacity, the lowest level since 2011 for this time of year, according to OilPrice citing Gas Infrastructure Europe data. Why it matters: Europe is heading into winter with its thinnest gas cushion in 15 years, and the Hormuz crisis means the usual LNG safety valve may not be available. If the Iran-Oman framework doesn't restore tanker traffic quickly, the EU's 90% fill target will be missed by a wide margin — making demand rationing likely in a cold scenario.
► Oil Rallies on Hormuz Uncertainty But Posts Worst Weekly Decline in Months Brent crude topped $83/barrel on Friday amid volatile trading driven by Hormuz deal headlines, but settled around $78. 2/barrel according to Trading Economics data — posting a weekly decline exceeding 7%, one of the steepest drops in months. Why it matters: The oil market is pricing in both a near-term risk premium from Hormuz disruption and a medium-term supply recovery if a deal holds — creating unusual volatility. The 7% weekly drop despite daily headline spikes suggests traders are positioning for a deal that restores flows, while the intraday rallies show how quickly that calculus could reverse.

Why it matters: The US is expanding the critical minerals toolkit beyond mining subsidies into outright export controls on processed and recycled materials — effectively treating refined minerals like a controlled technology.

item.title: Energy Brief: Europe Gas Storage at 14-Year Low as Winter Looms; Sinopec Ditches Middle East for Russian Crude; Libya Protests Shut Oil Fields
item.description:
European gas storage sits at just 57% — the lowest August level since 2011 — while Sinopec scoops up 300,000+ bpd of Russian ESPO crude to dodge Hormuz disruptions, Libya's energy sector buckles under protests and blackouts, and Iran says its Oman-negotiated Hormuz shipping route is in 'final stages' but warns it won't guarantee security.
► Europe Gas Storage at 2011 Lows as LNG Market Stays Squeezed EU gas storage sites were only 57% full as of August 5, the lowest level for this time of year since 2011 and well below the nearly 70% full storage at the same point in 2025, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe data reported by OilPrice. Why it matters: Europe is heading into winter with the thinnest gas cushion in 15 years. The Hormuz crisis isn't just about oil — it's gutting LNG supply too, and the backwardated market structure actively punishes storage. Without a major diplomatic breakthrough or a mild winter, Europe faces the real possibility of gas rationing.
► Iran-Oman Hormuz Route in 'Final Stages' — But Security Not Guaranteed Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Thursday that Iran and Oman have agreed on the 'geographical coordinates of the route' for commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, describing the deal as being in 'final stages of Why it matters: The gap between diplomatic optimism and maritime reality is as wide as ever. A 2-4 month temporary corridor with Iran controlling inbound traffic and charging transit fees is a major concession to Tehran — and markets are pricing in a reopening that shippers are not yet betting on.
► Sinopec Pivots to Russian ESPO Crude as Middle East Supply Unravels China's Sinopec, the world's largest refiner by capacity, has boosted purchases of Russian ESPO crude to 30-40 cargoes (241,000-320,000 bpd) for Q3 delivery, Reuters reported, citing trade sources and vessel-tracking data. Why it matters: The US waiver on Russian crude sanctions, originally a wartime expedient, is reshaping trade flows in ways that will outlast the conflict. China's largest refiner is now structurally dependent on Russian ESPO — a pipeline that gives Moscow both revenue and leverage.
► Libya Protests Force Oil Field Shutdowns as Grid Collapses Libya's energy sector is buckling under a compound crisis of blackouts, protests, and production shutdowns. Why it matters: Libya's energy sector is trapped in a feedback loop: political fragmentation prevents infrastructure investment, infrastructure failure triggers protests, protests shut down the oil and gas that funds the state, and production losses worsen the electricity crisis.
► US Diesel Exports Hit Record as Domestic Stocks Slide to 1996 Lows US diesel exports hit an all-time high of 1. 9 million barrels per day last week, according to EIA data reported by OilPrice, breaking the previous record set in spring. Why it matters: The US is running down its own diesel reserves to supply Europe and capitalize on record margins. With heating season approaching and refinery maintenance about to cut supply, this is a bet that the Hormuz crisis eases before winter. If it doesn't, diesel shortages could become a domestic political problem.
► UAE and Nigeria Fill the Gulf Vacuum — From Opposite Directions The UAE has managed to boost oil exports to pre-crisis levels by June, becoming the Gulf producer with the most crude exiting Hormuz, Bloomberg reported. Why it matters: The Hormuz crisis is accelerating a structural rebalancing of global crude flows. The UAE is monetizing its OPEC exit at record output, Nigeria is pushing toward 2 million bpd, and Angola is developing new offshore reserves — all positioning themselves as Hormuz-free alternatives.

item.title: Energy Brief: Houthis Strike Saudi Tanker in Red Sea as Hormuz Route Deal Takes Shape; Belarus Fuel Exports to Russia Hit Record; US Locks Down Critical Mineral Scrap
item.description:
Iran and Oman agree on Hormuz shipping route coordinates — but Tehran warns it alone won't guarantee security. Meanwhile, Houthis hit a Saudi tanker hundreds of kilometers from their declared blockade zone, Belarus replaces Russian refinery output lost to Ukrainian drones, and the US bans tungsten and battery black mass exports to keep critical minerals at home.
► Iran-Oman Agree on Hormuz Route Coordinates — But Security Remains Unresolved Iran and Oman have reached an 'understanding on the geographical coordinates of the route under discussion' for commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei announced on Wednesday, according t Why it matters: The route agreement is a genuine diplomatic step, but Iran's caveat that it doesn't guarantee security — combined with control over inbound traffic — means the strait's reopening would come on Tehran's terms. Markets are cautiously optimistic; shippers are not.
► Houthis Hit Saudi Tanker Far From Blockade Zone — Red Sea Threat Expands Yemen's Houthi movement claimed a 'precise hit' with ballistic missiles on the Saudi-flagged products tanker NCC WAFA off Yanbu in the northern Red Sea, hundreds of kilometers from the group's declared blockade zone around Bab el-Mandeb. Why it matters: The strike on a tanker near Yanbu — roughly 1,000 km north of Bab el-Mandeb — shows the Houthis can reach vessels attempting to evade their declared blockade zone. Rerouting north is no longer a safe mitigation. This compresses Saudi export options to Suez and the East-West pipeline further.
► Belarus Fuel Exports to Russia Hit Record as Ukrainian Drones Cripple Refineries Gasoline and diesel supplies from Belarus to Russia hit a new monthly record in July, according to Reuters, as fuel shortages driven by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to import from its neighbor. Why it matters: Ukraine's drone campaign has done what months of sanctions could not: force Russia to become a net fuel importer from its own client state and from countries as far as India and Morocco. The 25-fold increase in Belarusian gasoline shipments to Russia is a direct measure of how much refinery capacity has been lost.
► US Bans Tungsten and Battery Black Mass Exports to Secure Critical Mineral Supply The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security published an interim final rule on August 5 restricting exports of tungsten scrap and black mass — shredded metals from recycled lithium-ion batteries — for one year without a license. Why it matters: The US is now treating recycled battery metals and tungsten waste with the same export-control rigor as weapons-grade technology.
► China Eases Fuel Export Curbs for Second Month as Global Supply Squeezes China has eased limits on refined fuel exports for a second consecutive month in August, granting refiners temporary approval to ship 2. Why it matters: China's fuel export easing and the record refining margins at US refiners are two sides of the same coin: the Middle East conflict has created a massive geographic arbitrage in refined products. Refiners with access to stable crude flows are printing money while Gulf-dependent supply chains remain disrupted.
► Iraq-Syria Pipeline Could Bypass Hormuz Within Three Years A senior Syrian official says the old Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline from Iraq to Syria's Mediterranean coast could be up and running within three years, OilPrice reported. Why it matters: The Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline is a concrete response to the Hormuz crisis: a 1. 5-2 million bpd alternative that removes Iraqi dependency on the strait entirely. But three years is a long time in a conflict zone, and Syria's post-war governance raises questions about security of supply.
